# Why Your Company Should (Try to) Build Its Own AI SRE

## The Real Question Isn't Whether AI Can Do Incident Response — It's Whether Your Team Can Build One That Actually Works

The pitch is simple: let an AI agent handle root cause analysis so your on-call engineers can sleep. The reality is messier. But the underlying trend is real enough that your company should probably be experimenting with this now, even if the technology isn't fully baked.

---

## What's Actually Happening

In a recent episode of The New Stack podcast, Sam Farid and Nate Heinrich of Chronosphere made the case that AI agents should be deployed for root cause analysis during incidents. Their argument: as model capabilities improve, AI can help teams diagnose failures faster than humans scrolling through dashboards at 2 AM.

This isn't a new idea. SRE teams have been automating runbooks and building alert correlation tools for years. What's different now is the claim that general-purpose AI models — or fine-tuned versions of them — can actually reason about system failures in ways that go beyond pattern matching.

Chronosphere isn't alone here. The observability space has been racing to bolt AI capabilities onto existing platforms. The promise is always the same: reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR), cut down on alert fatigue, and free up senior engineers from firefighting.

But here's what caught my attention in the podcast discussion: Farid and Heinrich aren't just talking about AI as a helper that surfaces possible causes. They're talking about AI agents that can actively investigate — pulling metrics, checking logs, correlating events across services. The agent doesn't just suggest; it digs.

That's a meaningful shift. And it raises a question most companies haven't seriously considered: should you try to build something like this yourself?

---

## Why Practitioners Should Care

Let's be honest about the current state of on-call work.

Most incident response still looks like this: an alert fires, someone gets paged, they open a dozen tabs, they start grepping logs, they check recent deploys, they ask in Slack if anyone changed anything, and eventually they either find the problem or escalate. The process works, but it's slow and it burns people out.

AI-assisted root cause analysis promises to compress that timeline. Instead of a human manually correlating signals, an AI agent could do the initial triage — pulling relevant metrics, identifying anomalies, checking for recent changes, and presenting a hypothesis for the engineer to validate or reject.

The appeal is obvious. But the gap between "this sounds useful" and "this actually works in production" is where things get interesting.

### The Build vs. Buy Question

Most companies will buy an AI SRE capability rather than build one. Observability vendors are shipping these features, and for many teams that's the right call. You get integration with your existing tooling, you don't have to train models, and someone else handles the maintenance.

But there's a case for building your own, even if it's just a proof of concept:

**1. Your systems are unique.** Generic models don't know your architecture. They don't know that Service A always gets slow when Team B deploys, or that the database connection pool warnings are usually false positives. A model trained on your incident history, your runbooks, and your system topology might be more useful than a generic one — or it might not. You won't know until you try.

**2. You control the context window.** The biggest limitation of AI agents right now is context. They can only reason about what they can see. If you build your own system, you decide what gets fed to the model. You can include internal documentation, past incident reports, architecture diagrams, and tribal knowledge that a vendor tool will never have.

**3. You build institutional knowledge.** The process of building an AI SRE — even a basic one — forces you to codify what your team actually knows about your systems. That's valuable even if the AI itself turns out to be mediocre.

**4. You can iterate faster.** Vendor roadmaps don't align with your priorities. If you build your own tooling, you can experiment with different approaches without waiting for a feature request to make it through product planning.

### The Risks of Building

Building your own AI SRE isn't free. The obvious costs are engineering time and compute resources. But there are less obvious risks too.

**Hallucinations in incident response are dangerous.** An AI that confidently points at the wrong root cause can send your team down a rabbit hole while the actual problem gets worse. In high-stakes incidents, bad information is worse than no information.

**Maintenance burden.** Models drift. Systems change. An AI SRE that worked great six months ago might become useless — or actively harmful — as your architecture evolves. Someone has to own the ongoing calibration.

**Security and access.** For an AI agent to do meaningful investigation, it needs access to your observability data, your logs, your deployment history, maybe even your code. That's a significant attack surface to manage.

None of these are reasons not to try. But they're reasons to be realistic about what you're signing up for.

---

## [CHRIS TAKE]

---

## What to Watch / What to Do Next

If you're considering building an AI SRE capability — even as an experiment — here's where I'd focus:

### Start Small and Specific

Don't try to build a general-purpose incident response agent. Pick a narrow use case. Maybe it's a bot that automatically pulls the last 24 hours of relevant metrics when a specific alert fires. Maybe it's a tool that summarizes the most likely causes based on recent changes. Scope it tightly, measure whether it helps, and iterate from there.

### Ground the Model in Your Data

The value of a custom AI SRE comes from context. Feed it your incident postmortems. Feed it your runbooks. Feed it your architecture documentation. The more specific the context, the more useful the output. Generic models give generic answers.

### Build for Human-in-the-Loop

Don't automate remediation. Not yet. AI should be surfacing information and hypotheses, not executing fixes. Your engineers should be validating every suggestion. This isn't just about safety — it's about building trust. If the AI is right 80% of the time, people will learn when to trust it. If it's right 50% of the time, they'll learn to ignore it.

### Measure Honestly

Track whether the AI actually reduces time to diagnosis. Track how often engineers follow its suggestions versus ignore them. Track how often it's wrong. You need real data to decide whether this is worth continuing.

### Watch the Vendor Space

Even if you build something internally, keep an eye on what observability vendors are shipping. The technology is moving fast. What's impossible today might be turnkey in 18 months. Your internal experiments will help you evaluate vendor offerings more critically when the time comes.

### Security Review Everything

If your AI agent has access to logs, metrics, or deployment data, treat it like any other system with elevated privileges. Review the access controls. Log what it's doing. Think about what happens if the model itself gets compromised or manipulated. [UNVERIFIED — I haven't seen detailed threat models published for AI agents with observability access, but this seems like an obvious gap.]

---

## The Talent and Process Angle

Building an AI SRE isn't just a technical project. It's also a people project.

Who owns this system? Is it the SRE team? The platform team? A dedicated ML engineering group? The answer matters because it determines how the system evolves and who's accountable when it breaks.

How do you handle the transition? On-call engineers have existing workflows. Adding an AI assistant changes those workflows. Some people will adopt it immediately; others will resist. You need to think about training, feedback loops, and how you'll measure whether people are actually using it.

What happens to the team structure over time? If AI can do 30% of the incident triage work, does that mean you need fewer on-call engineers, or does it mean the same engineers can handle more services? The answer depends on your organization, but it's worth thinking through before you're surprised by the implications.

---

## The Broader Industry Context

This trend isn't happening in isolation. AI agents for operations fit into a larger shift toward autonomous systems that can act, not just observe.

We've seen this pattern before with automation. Configuration management tools, auto-scaling policies, self-healing infrastructure — each generation of automation took tasks that humans used to do and encoded them in software. AI agents are the next step, applying reasoning to situations that are too dynamic or complex for traditional rule-based automation.

The question is whether the models are actually good enough. Farid and Heinrich are bullish — they argue that model capabilities are improving fast enough that root cause analysis is becoming tractable. Others are more skeptical, pointing out that reasoning about complex distributed systems is fundamentally different from the tasks that current AI models excel at.

I don't think anyone knows for sure. Which is exactly why experimentation matters. The companies that try this now will learn things — about their systems, about their teams, about the technology — that will give them an advantage when the technology matures.

---

## A Note on Vendor Claims

Every observability vendor is going to tell you their AI features are production-ready. Some of them might be. But be skeptical.

Ask specific questions: What data does the model train on? How do you handle customer data privacy? What's the latency for an AI-assisted diagnosis? How often does the model give incorrect or misleading suggestions? How do you handle model updates when my system changes?

If the vendor can't give you concrete answers, they're probably still figuring it out themselves.

---

## Where This Could Go

The optimistic scenario: AI agents become standard infrastructure, like dashboards and alerting pipelines are today. On-call engineers work alongside AI assistants that handle the routine investigation work, freeing humans to focus on the novel and complex problems.

The pessimistic scenario: AI SRE turns out to be a lot of hype. Models can't reliably reason about distributed systems. Teams waste months building tooling that doesn't work. Vendor features get quietly deprecated.

The realistic scenario: it's somewhere in between. AI helps in some situations and fails in others. Teams that invest early learn which use cases work and which don't. The technology improves incrementally. In five years, some version of AI-assisted incident response becomes normal, but it looks different from what anyone is pitching today.

---

## Closing Thought

The case for building your own AI SRE isn't about whether the technology is ready. It's about whether you want to be learning now or catching up later.

Most experiments will fail. That's fine. The point is to build enough intuition about what works — and what doesn't — that you can make better decisions as the technology matures.

So here's the question worth asking at your next architecture review: What would an AI SRE need to know about your systems to be useful, and how much of that knowledge currently lives only in your engineers' heads?
